title: SYSK Selects: How Wills Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "How Wills Work." Josh and Chuck open with banter about favorite show lines and the 1979 film Scavenger Hunt, then cover will basics (what to include, Staples do-it-yourself forms, state law, sound mind requirements, choosing an executor), the types of wills (oral, deathbed, holographic, DIY, ironclad/self-proving), changing and challenging wills, disinheriting children and spouses (in terrorem clauses), estate and "death tax" issues, trusts, living wills, and odd celebrity and historical bequests. The episode closes with listener mail from a listener asking the hosts to help reunite a couple.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, How Wills Work. He and Chuck trade banter about favorite show lines and 1979 movies, and Josh recommends the film Scavenger Hunt, which he says involves Vincent Price and a will.

segments.title: Basics of writing a will
segments.summary: The hosts say a will is not hard to draw up, state law governs wills, and forms are available at Staples. They list key contents: names of spouse and children, a revocation clause, executor and alternate, special gifts, debt instructions, and burial wishes. They note pensions and life insurance pass by beneficiary designation and need not be in the will.

segments.title: Eligibility and sound mind
segments.summary: Most states require the testator to be at least 18 and of sound mind. The hosts explain that sound mind means knowing one's property and family, and that a later mental illness does not invalidate a will made while of sound mind.

segments.title: Choosing an executor
segments.summary: The executor inventories the estate, pays legitimate debts, and distributes assets under the will. The hosts advise choosing someone trustworthy, thoughtful, and organized, and name an alternate.

segments.title: Types of wills: oral, deathbed, holographic, DIY, ironclad
segments.summary: The hosts describe oral wills, often made by dying soldiers before two witnesses, and deathbed wills, which are frequently challenged over mental capacity. Holographic handwritten wills are not recognized in every state. They also cover DIY forms and ironclad, lawyer-drafted, self-proving wills with witness affidavits.

segments.title: Changing and challenging wills
segments.summary: Wills can be changed by the testator through a new will, a revocation, or a codicil. The hosts explain who has standing to challenge a will and common grounds such as coercion, fraud, undue influence, or improper execution, noting such challenges are difficult and expensive.

segments.title: Disinheriting children and spouses; estate and death taxes; trusts
segments.summary: The hosts explain that a child can be disinherited with a specific statement, while spouses generally receive a share and an in terrorem clause is used to discourage challenges. They discuss estate taxes called the death tax by opponents, with a 2006 example, and mention trusts for avoiding probate and managing a minor's assets.

segments.title: Living wills
segments.summary: The hosts describe a living will as a document about medical treatment rather than property, often paired with a power of attorney for health decisions.

segments.title: Unusual and celebrity wills
segments.summary: The hosts recount odd bequests: a Portuguese aristocrat leaving one-dollar bills to strangers, a composer's opera offered to the Metropolitan Opera, a Nokia founder's shares left to nursing home residents, Frisbee designer Ed Headrick's ashes, Mark Gruenwald's ashes in ink, Dusty Springfield's cat provision, Leona Helmsley's dog bequest, and a tree in Athens that owns itself.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts read a listener email asking them to help a listener named Timmy reunite with his girlfriend Elaine, and then ask listeners to send stories of crazy will stipulations.
